PullRequest.Title: Support Marketplace-native deprecation for extensions
PullRequest.Body: Consumes Marketplace deprecation metadata, preferring API records and falling back per extension to `marketplace.json` control file when Marketplace does not provide deprecation details. Updates extension details, install confirmations, and `@deprecated` results as metadata changes. Shows replacement guidance alongside safely rendered publisher messages. Adds the hidden, default-on `extensions.experimental.marketplaceDeprecation` setting for live rollback to legacy-only behavior. Includes regression coverage for response normalization, precedence, metadata refresh, rollback, and rendering. To test, compare API-only, legacy-only, and conflicting deprecation records with the setting enabled and disabled. Testing requires a Marketplace instance with the Deprecation feature enabled (or a proxy to intercept and add the deprecation properties). I also provided a mock control file to match extension identities. Test scenarios covered: 1. Extension deprecated on Marketplace only 2. Extension deprecated in control file (marketplace.json) only 3. Extension deprecated on Marketplace and in control file (Marketplace data wins) 4. Non-deprecated extension The Marketplace provides a publisher message "Marketplace deprecated" for Extension 1 and 3; Extension 3 also provides a replacement extension. The control file provides a publisher message "LEGACY fallback message" for extensions 2 and 3. Screenshots from testing (feature setting enabled): * Extensions 1-3 all show disabled with no install gesture available: * Extensions 1 and 3 show Marketplace deprecation data (note for 3, the control file message is overshadowed by Marketplace data) | Extension 1 | Extension 3 | |-|-| | | | * Extension 2 shows control file data With the feature setting disabled, only extension 2 and 3 are shown as disabled, and both have the LEGACY fallback message:

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The event producer, refresh path, collection scan, and model replacement are directly traced. Only the exact duration varies by extension count and server latency.
Findings.PerformanceResource: CPU work, PagedModel allocations, and list rendering
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Every accepted undefined event scans all installed extensions, sorts matching rows, and replaces the list model; queryLocal can emit one event for each local, remote, and web extension server.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased refresh latency and avoidable list rendering.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Generic undefined workbench invalidations were ignored; only events carrying an installed extension refreshed this model.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: An @deprecated view now accepts every undefined workbench change and unconditionally publishes a newly filtered PagedModel.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added `(isDeprecatedQuery && !e)` at line 349 broadens the listener to all untyped invalidations; the added deprecated-query branch later in the same hunk always returns `newExtensions`, causing model publication.
Findings.Title: Restrict deprecated-list refreshes to relevant changes
Findings.Impact: Refreshing the Extensions view while @deprecated is open first runs queryLocal, whose per-server queryInstalled calls emit undefined, then runs the explicit search refresh. This can rebuild the list during inventory loading and rebuild it again for the search; unrelated auto-update or install-completion invalidations do the same. Cost grows with installed extensions and configured extension servers.
Findings.Evidence: queryLocal sequentially calls queryInstalled for each server (extensionsWorkbenchService.ts:1535-1570), and queryInstalled fires undefined (line 748). ExtensionsViewlet.refresh awaits queryLocal before doSearch(true) (extensionsViewlet.ts:762-766). This callback filters/sorts local extensions and fires a new PagedModel (extensionsViews.ts:352-359); updateModel replaces the list's DelayedPagedModel (lines 1098-1101).
Findings.Recommendation: Use a deprecation-specific/configuration event or tag the invalidation reason, retain concrete installed-extension events, and avoid publishing when deprecated identifiers and order are unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: Marketplace gallery search, paging, and direct extension lookup
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The existing Marketplace HTTP query/getExtensions request must complete; deprecation normalization then runs inline once per returned gallery record before results are exposed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Marketplace extension query or batched getExtensions request
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One existing request per page or batched lookup; not one request per extension.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same request returned and normalized gallery records without copying deprecation fields.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The response is already required before gallery models can be returned.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Returned gallery records per page or batched identifier lookup; normalization adds constant work and a small object only for records carrying deprecation metadata.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Existing request and paging behavior is unchanged; no new per-record requests or concurrency burst is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Existing gallery/request behavior is unchanged. Deprecation data arrives in the same response, so cold and warm behavior add no separate lookup or negative-cache state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed conversion code and tests show deprecation is mapped from the existing payload with no additional request.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Publisher-message lengths and page sizes vary, but the added per-record normalization is bounded and does not change request cardinality.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression; the new metadata does not add a boundary or meaningful scaling mechanism.

Scenarios.Scenario: Installed-extension inventory and Marketplace metadata synchronization/check-for-updates
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Existing installed-inventory IPC/filesystem reads and batched Marketplace update checks complete before synchronized models are current; compatibility lookup remains on its pre-existing path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read the extensions control manifest and installed extension inventory
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One control-manifest call and one getInstalled call per configured extension server for each queryLocal inventory refresh.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same inventory refresh performed these calls and emitted an undefined change after each server.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Inventory refresh waits for these existing calls.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Fetch latest/compatible Marketplace extension records during update checks
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Existing batched latest-version request plus compatibility work only for extensions requiring it; no new deprecation-only request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same update/compatibility path refreshed versions and blocking metadata.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Update synchronization already waited for this work; deprecation is consumed from the same records.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Installed extensions, grouped by extension identity; metadata equality checks are constant-size per matched model, while notifications occur only when effective metadata changes.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Server inventories are queried sequentially by queryLocal; compatibility checks retain their existing Promise.allSettled behavior and batched gallery fetches.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The control manifest retains its five-minute cache. Marketplace deprecation is retained on each model and equivalent records are coalesced by deep equality; omitted/failed gallery results preserve prior metadata.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed code only stores/compares deprecation fields from existing gallery objects and combines change notifications.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of installed extensions and incompatible versions varies, but no new boundary cardinality was introduced.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate regression in synchronization; notification coalescing prevents duplicate events for equivalent metadata.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open and refresh the local @deprecated extensions result
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Initial display waits for queryLocal inventory. A manual Extensions refresh again waits for per-server inventory, then performs an explicit search refresh. The changed listener also rebuilds the visible deprecated model from generic undefined events during this path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Fetch control manifest and installed inventory for each configured extension server
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One pair per configured server per queryLocal call; local, remote, and web servers are processed sequentially.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The calls and undefined completion events existed, but @deprecated did not subscribe to every undefined event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The refresh waits for these existing calls, and their completion events now fan into redundant list reconstruction before the explicit doSearch(true).

Scenarios.ScalingInput: All installed extensions are scanned; deprecated matches are sorted and published. Work repeats with accepted invalidations and can occur once per local/remote/web server when server calls are separated beyond the 100 ms debounce.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: queryLocal queries configured servers sequentially. Event.debounce coalesces events within 100 ms but does not guarantee coalescing across sequential remote inventory calls; each delivered event performs a full synchronous filter/sort and model replacement.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The PR removes the direct control-manifest lookup from filterDeprecatedExtensions and reads model metadata instead. However, queryLocal still refreshes server inventory/control data; generic undefined events are not keyed or deduplicated by deprecation result identity.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: event producer, listener broadening, collection work, and model replacement were directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact UI delay depends on installed/deprecated counts and server latency; the repeated scan/model replacement and refresh reachability are deterministic.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable repeated rendering work: the new broad undefined-event subscription rebuilds the deprecated list for unrelated/global invalidations.

Scenarios.Scenario: Extension details/list status, hover, install confirmation, and Marketplace rollback toggle
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Status computation and Markdown rendering occur locally when a row/detail status is recomputed, a hover opens, or an install confirmation is shown. The hidden feature toggle synchronously invalidates existing models but performs no network lookup.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One extension status at a time for details/hover; visible list rows scale with rendered rows. Publisher Markdown adds one additional local render only when Marketplace deprecation includes a message.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Status recomputation remains serialized by the existing Throttler; hover render disposables are cleared before replacement, so rendered nodes/listeners do not accumulate.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Effective deprecation is selected from retained Marketplace and legacy records on each access; toggle changes reuse retained records and need no cache refill.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for local rendering/lifecycle; no changed subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network boundary was found on these UI paths.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Publisher-message size is Marketplace-controlled, but no evidence establishes realistically unbounded content or repeated offscreen rendering.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression; additional Markdown is demand-driven and disposed on rerender/hover replacement.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 11 changed files and relevant callers. One diff-introduced repeated-work issue was submitted for broad @deprecated invalidation fan-in. Gallery metadata transport, installed synchronization, UI Markdown lifecycle, caches, request cardinality, and effective concurrency otherwise introduce no actionable performance regression.
